cards.explanation: The answer is False. This time Balaam skips the omens. The text says he “…did not seek omens as on previous occasions…” (Numbers 24:1). Verse 1 ties it to what he saw, that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel. So Balaam drops the old routine.

The answer is wilderness. Balaam turns his face toward the wilderness instead of going off for omens. From there he lifts his eyes and sees Israel camped tribe by tribe. Nice and simple, friends. Sometimes the answer is just where the text points.

The answer is Spirit. The Spirit of God comes upon Balaam, and verse 2 says it happens as he looks up and sees Israel encamped tribe by tribe. Then he lifts up an oracle, a spoken message, and the words that follow in verses 3 to 9 are what he says.

The answer is gardens and trees growing by water. Verse 6 says Israel's camp is spread out “…like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.” That's a whole lot of green, friends. Every picture he picks is a growing thing.

The answer is True, and verse 7 says it plainly: “His king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted.” The text names Agag here and gives nothing more about him in this passage. So Israel's king comes out greater. That's a lot of good news from a man who was hired to deliver bad news.

The answer is that they are cursed themselves. Verse 9 ends, “Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.” Now think about who invited Balaam out here to curse Israel. Balak, king of Moab, is standing right there hearing it.

The answer is three. Balak says, “I summoned you to curse my enemies, but behold, you have persisted in blessing them these three times.” He's been keeping score, and he is not happy with the total. When someone keeps count out loud like that, you know the patience is gone.

The answer is that Balak tells Balaam to flee at once to his home. His words are, “Therefore, flee at once to your home!” He adds that he said he would reward Balaam richly, but the LORD has denied the reward. He's done with the hilltops, the oracles and Balaam. That's what a king sounds like when he's out of patience.

The answer is True, and it's Balak himself who says it. Verse 11 reads, “I said I would reward you richly, but instead the LORD has denied your reward.” Even Balak, with his anger burning, names the LORD as the reason the reward isn't coming. I think that's quite an admission to make in that mood.

The answer is going beyond the command of the LORD. In verse 13 Balaam says that even if Balak gave him his house full of silver and gold, he could not do anything of his own accord, good or bad, to go beyond the LORD's command. Then he adds, “I must speak whatever the LORD says.” A whole house full of silver and gold, friends, and the answer is still no.

The answer is a warning about what Israel will do to Moab. Balaam says, “…let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come.” Balak is the king of Moab, so those are Balak's people. Balaam is leaving, but he's not leaving quietly.

The answer is that he's coming later on. Balaam says, “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.” Not now and not near both point to a time down the road. He's looking ahead, and it isn't today.

The answer is a king rising up from Israel. Verse 17 says, “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel.” Then verse 19 adds, “A ruler will come from Jacob…” Star, scepter and ruler all point the same way.

The answer is Moab. Verse 17 says, “He will crush the skulls of Moab…” Balak is king of Moab, so Balaam is delivering this news right to his face. Hard moment for him to hear, friends, and he's the one who asked for this guy to come.

The answer is True. Verse 18 says, “Edom will become a possession, as will Seir, his enemy…” Edom is the nation that came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). Balaam is just going down the list, one nation after another.

The answer is destruction. Verse 20 says, “Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction.” Balaam gives Amalek a big title, and then that little word “but” swings the whole line around. Watch for the turn, friends, because that's what matters here.

The answer is False, because the text doesn't promise that. Verse 21 says, “Your dwelling place is secure, and your nest is set in a cliff.” Then verse 22 says, “Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” That little word “yet” is where the good news stops.

The answer is Asshur. Verse 22 says, “Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” It's a short name in a short line, but the line is heavy. A secure place on a cliff, and then a captor.

The answer is perish. Verse 24 says, “Ships will come from the coasts of Cyprus; they will subdue Asshur and Eber, but they too will perish forever.” Notice the “too” in there. Even the ones who come out on top in this line don't stay on top.

The answer is True, friends. Verse 25 says, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” Balak had summoned Balaam to curse Israel, and now the two of them part, each heading his own direction. After all those big oracles, I think it's a pretty quiet exit. The story of Balaam and Balak ends here.
